objective: Học xong bài này, bạn sẽ nhận diện được quan điểm của tác giả để trả lời YNNG, và lấy đúng chi tiết về các khâu của chuỗi lạnh trong bài đọc về vận chuyển thực phẩm và thuốc.

sentences.text: Every day, enormous quantities of food and medicine travel across the world in a condition that most consumers never think about: cold.
Fresh fish, frozen vegetables, vaccines and many other products lose quality or become unsafe if their temperature rises even briefly above a safe limit.
To prevent this, producers, transport companies and retailers maintain an unbroken sequence of refrigerated storage and transport known as the cold chain.
From the moment a product is chilled after production until the moment it is used, every link in the chain, each warehouse, lorry and container, must hold it within a set temperature range.
If a single link fails, everything that passed through it may have to be thrown away, however valuable it is.
Behind the scenes, an entire global industry of insulated ships, refrigerated warehouses and trained handlers exists for the single purpose of keeping that sequence unbroken.
A typical journey begins with pre-cooling, which removes the warmth of the field or the factory before goods are packed for transport.
The products then travel in refrigerated lorries to a cold store, where they may wait before being loaded into refrigerated containers for the sea crossing.
At the destination port, inspectors check seals and temperature records before the containers are released to distributors.
Small refrigerated vans complete the final stage, known as the last mile, delivering to shops, restaurants and clinics.
Throughout the journey, electronic sensors fixed inside the packaging record the temperature every few minutes, creating a history that buyers can examine on arrival.
Every transfer between these stages is recorded as well, so that if something goes wrong, investigators can identify exactly where the temperature first escaped its range.
In practice, the chain most often breaks not in the middle of an ocean crossing but at the points where goods change hands.
Pallets may wait on a hot loading dock while paperwork is completed, or a container may sit unplugged during a long customs delay.
A few hours of warmth can be enough to spoil a load of berries or to weaken a batch of vaccines, yet the damage is frequently invisible when the goods arrive.
This pattern suggests that the weakest point of the cold chain is not refrigeration technology, which is reliable and widely available, but the handovers between companies.
Each handover involves a different firm, and responsibility for the temperature can become unclear precisely when the risk of damage is greatest.
New technology is now being aimed at exactly these weak points in the chain.
Data loggers that send live readings to a control centre allow managers to react while a load can still be saved, instead of discovering the problem afterwards.
In regions where the electricity supply is unreliable, solar-powered cold rooms let farmers and clinics store produce and medicines without depending on the grid.
Reusable packaging filled with cooling materials can hold a safe temperature for several days without any power supply at all.
Drones are even being tested to carry small, urgent medical deliveries across areas where the roads are poor.
Trials of delivery drones in parts of East Africa have already cut the time needed to reach remote clinics from hours to minutes.
Keeping the world cold is expensive, and refrigeration also consumes large amounts of energy wherever it is used.
There is therefore a tension at the heart of the cold chain: widening it protects health and cuts food waste, but it also adds to emissions.
In my view, this tension does not justify slowing the spread of cold chains to poorer regions, where losses after harvest are highest.
The greater priority is to make each link cleaner and more reliable, using renewable power and better insulation materials.
If the handovers can be fixed, the chain will finally be as strong as the technology that built it.
The direction of the industry is therefore towards chains that are not only unbroken, but cleaner at every link.

explanation.whyWrong: Không phải NOT GIVEN vì quan điểm được khẳng định trực tiếp bằng câu có cụm 'In my view'.

evidence.quote: This pattern suggests that the weakest point of the cold chain is not refrigeration technology, which is reliable and widely available, but the handovers between companies.

explanation.trap: Cấu trúc 'not X but Y' đảo chiều hoàn toàn: phần bị phủ định là công nghệ, phần được khẳng định là khâu bàn giao.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tác giả viết điểm yếu nhất không phải công nghệ làm lạnh, vốn đáng tin cậy và phổ biến, mà là các khâu bàn giao giữa công ty.
explanation.whyWrong: Không phải YES vì bài nói ngược lại. Không phải NOT GIVEN vì tác giả đánh giá độ tin cậy của công nghệ một cách rõ ràng.

explanation.whyWrong: Đáp án là đại lượng được đo, tức nhiệt độ; 'history' là sản phẩm của việc ghi, không đứng sau động từ 'record' trong cấu trúc này.

sentences.text: Long before mechanical refrigeration, traders understood that cold preserved food, and a valuable trade in natural ice grew up during the nineteenth century.
Blocks of ice were cut from frozen lakes in winter, stored in insulated ice houses packed with sawdust, and shipped as far away as India and Australia.
Salt was used to lower the temperature of ice still further, allowing fish and meat to be frozen hard for long journeys by rail.
Early refrigerated railway wagons carried a supply of ice at each end, which porters replaced at stations along the route.
At its height, the trade employed thousands of workers in ice harvesting alone, and the quality of a shipment could decide whether a distant town ate fresh fish or went without.
These methods worked, but they were slow, heavy and limited by the weather, since a mild winter meant a shortage of ice the following summer.
Merchants also had no way of knowing the temperature their goods had experienced, because nothing was recorded during the journey.
When mechanical refrigeration arrived, it did not merely make the old trade colder; it made temperature controllable and, eventually, measurable.
The modern cold chain therefore began not with a single invention but with the replacement of harvested ice by machines.
Historians of technology often note that the demand for ice also drove improvements in insulation, packaging and railway design that outlived the trade itself.
In that sense, the cold chain is older than the machines that now define it.
